unit.title: Swift bootcamp: programs and collections
unit.summary: Start with small Swift files. Learn numbers, choices, functions, and collections before adding an iOS framework.

lessons.title: Write and run your first Swift program
lessons.summary: Write a small Swift file, run it on your computer, and explain what the code and build tools each do.
objectives: Run a Swift file and explain what each line does.
Tell source text, a runnable program, and the tools that build it apart.
Find whether a first failure comes from the code, the command, or the output.

sections.title: Start with one small calculation
sections.html:
A source file is a text file with instructions for a program. A compiler checks those instructions and translates them into code the computer can run. You can try a Kotlin calculation before adding an Android screen. You can start Swift just as simply. First predict one result. Then run the file and compare. Your engineering experience helps you ask useful questions; this lesson assumes no Swift syntax, Apple framework knowledge, or iOS project setup.

Today’s program prints a made-up booking caption. It has no network, company data, screen, or credentials. Save it in your own scratch directory as First.swift; the filename suffix tells tools and readers which language the text contains. An editor is enough to author it. Xcode is Apple’s IDE and includes platform tools, but opening an iOS project is unnecessary for this host exercise. A host is the computer executing the program, here macOS. A successful host run establishes this little program’s behavior; it does not establish an iOS build or installation.

sections.title: Read the six lines in order
sections.html:
A binding gives a value a name. In this program, let creates a binding you cannot assign again. var creates one you can change. A String holds text, and an integer holds a whole number. The comment starts with // and is for the reader. The program names the learner Sam, starts attempts at one, adds one, builds a caption, and prints it. Swift works out the types from these starting values; this is called type inference.

// A synthetic caption, run as one file.
let learner = "Sam"
var attempts = 1
attempts = attempts + 1
let caption = "Hello, \(learner). Attempt \(attempts)."
print(caption)

Line four reads the current attempts, adds one, and assigns the result back. Assignment uses one equals sign; a comparison will use two. Line five constructs a new string. Within quoted text, \(expression) inserts the printable representation of an expression; this is called interpolation. Swift uses that syntax instead of Kotlin’s dollar interpolation. Line six calls the standard-library function print. Parentheses enclose its argument, caption. The expected single line is Hello, Sam. Attempt 2.. Swift usually needs no semicolon at a line’s end. Keep the order: the later caption uses the already updated integer.

sections.title: Run the text, then build a program file
sections.html:
An executable is a file the computer can run. Source text is the editable recipe; the executable is a result of building that recipe. Run these commands in the folder holding First.swift. swift --version names the selected tools. swift First.swift compiles and runs the text. swiftc builds an executable, and -o First names it. ./First runs that file from the current folder. Both routes should print the same caption. A missing file and rejected Swift syntax need different repairs.

swift --version
swift First.swift
swiftc First.swift -o First
./First

On macOS, xcrun swift --version can inspect Swift through Apple’s selected developer tools. Tool selection depends on the local setup; record the command and observed version instead of memorizing the author’s machine. Later lessons use modern syntax such as explicit any and some; a Swift 6 or newer scratch toolchain is a simple baseline for this sequence. No package or remote dependency is needed here. If command-line tools are absent, keep your predictions and diagnose installation separately. Do not clear shared caches or alter client build settings to make this six-line example run.

sections.title: Know what each version number describes
sections.html:
A toolchain is the set of tools used to build code, including the compiler. Its version tells you which language features it understands. Language mode selects supported checking rules for your source. A package tools-version header sets its minimum package tools and manifest API. A manifest is the file describing what the package builds. An SDK supplies platform declarations at build time. A deployment target sets the oldest supported OS for that component. These numbers answer separate questions, just as Kotlin, JVM target, Android SDK, and minimum Android version do.

A Swift package groups targets, dependencies, and products. A target is a component built by the tools, often also a module you can import. A dependency is another component it needs. A product offers built targets to users of the package. An Xcode scheme chooses actions and configurations for targets. These resemble parts of a Gradle build, but schemes are not exact product flavors and packages are not AARs. Our small file uses the standard library, which supplies String, Int, and print. UIKit is an iOS UI framework. Adding import UIKit would change which platform can build the file; it is unnecessary for this host calculation.

sections.title: Separate rejected code from wrong output
sections.html:
A diagnostic is a message explaining a problem the compiler found. Try predicting one for learner = "Lee": learner was declared with let, so assignment fails before the program runs. Use var when the requirement calls for a later change. Making every binding mutable removes helpful checks. A misspelling such as captin names no known binding. A missing closing quote breaks parsing, the step that reads code structure. If the shell cannot find swift or First.swift, check tools or paths instead.

Code can pass the compiler and still give the wrong answer. If you build the caption before adding one, it records attempt one. That String does not keep watching attempts. The same timing issue can occur when a Kotlin string template is made before its input changes. Write the expected line first, then compare it with the run. Save the command, the first useful diagnostic or output, and the rule you think explains it. Keep rejected experiments in separate scratch files so the working version remains available. A passing script checks this behavior; it does not establish persistence, safe thread access, or screen lifetime.

sections.title: Find the same pieces in real source
sections.html:
A repository anchor points to a specific file and line you can inspect. Open the linked package and target declarations after running your small file. The package tools header says 5.9; the iOS platform says 17. They describe different requirements. The cancellation target builds an iOS static framework and lists the source files it includes. That file pattern, called a source glob, connects the question model to the target. Seeing a folder alone would not prove it is built. Reading these lines does not prove the company app builds.

In CancelAppointmentQuestionData, read let key: String as an immutable property with an explicit type. A property belongs to an instance of a named type, whereas learner in our program is a local/top-level binding. You will learn those containers later. For now, identify the familiar declaration pieces without understanding every surrounding type. Imported company modules are not needed for any beginner exercise. A main companion may provide a host package at labs/SwiftLanguageLab; its concrete APIs must be read before use. This lesson’s standalone source remains the runnable contract even if that companion is absent.

exercise.brief: Write your own caption. Change the name, update a counter twice, and save the source and output.
steps: Create a scratch Swift file. Use let for a name and var for a counter starting at zero.
Add one twice. Then build and print a caption.
Predict what the caption would say if you built it before the second update.
In a separate copy, try assigning a new value to the let name. Save the compiler message.
Write three sentences explaining a host run, a tools version, and an iOS deployment target.
acceptance: The final working caption contains your synthetic name and counter two.
Every declaration, interpolation and call is explained without relying on Kotlin syntax.

exercise.solution:
Try your own program first. The worked answer below runs as one file and uses Rae as its input. An import brings another module into scope; this program needs none. Save it with your chosen filename and use the same run commands. Before running, predict the two printed lines. Notice where each caption is made relative to the counter updates.

let name = "Rae"
var counter = 0
counter = counter + 1
let early = "\(name): \(counter)"
counter = counter + 1
let finalCaption = "\(name): \(counter)"
print(early)
print(finalCaption)

The outputs are Rae: 1 and Rae: 2. Name stays fixed, counter permits assignments, and each String records its construction-time value. The early value does not change after the second update. Reassigning name would fail compilation, while changing the initial literal is permitted when you edit and rerun source. Explain both distinctions.

Your verification note can say that a selected Swift toolchain compiled and ran this standalone host file. The inspected package header names a minimum tools requirement, and its iOS platform declaration constrains that client target. Neither statement proves the client built. Keep the learner’s attempt pending until they have produced their own source and evidence; this worked answer is reference material.

lessons.title: Choose types and handle numbers, text, and missing values
lessons.summary: Choose the right kind of value, calculate an average, and keep a missing label separate from an empty label.
objectives: Read the type after a colon and choose a suitable number type.
Predict arithmetic, comparisons, text construction, and which conditions run.
Handle a value that may be missing with an explicit fallback.

sections.title: Say what kind of value you need
sections.html:
A type says what kind of value a name can hold and which operations it supports. A form summary may need a whole-number count, a fractional average, and a label that can be missing. Swift keeps those choices visible. let count: Int = 3 gives count the whole-number type Int. The colon introduces a type annotation, an explicit type name. let count = 3 lets Swift infer Int from the value. Inference still gives a fixed type; it does not let count become arbitrary text later.

Int stores native-size signed whole numbers. Explicit widths such as Int64 state a fixed number of bits. Double stores floating-point numbers, Bool stores true or false, and String stores text. Character holds one extended grapheme cluster, the Unicode group Swift treats as one character. The context can make a number literal a Double; this is different from automatically converting an existing Int variable. Kotlin Int is always 32 bits. Swift Int follows the platform width and is 64 bits on this Apple host. Use Int64 for an explicitly signed 64-bit wire value and Int for ordinary local counts. A fitting type still does not validate a product rule.

sections.title: Convert before you divide
sections.html:
Integer division keeps only the whole-number part, rounding toward zero. Seven divided by two as integers is three. A Double can hold a fractional result. Double(total) and Double(count) convert the operands before division, giving 3.5. Converting the integer answer afterward gives 3.0; the lost fraction cannot return. The remainder operator % gives one here. With negative input, its sign follows the number being divided, called the dividend. Keep that rule separate from a mathematical modulo rule.

let total: Int = 7
let count: Int = 2
let whole = total / count
let average = Double(total) / Double(count)
let remainder = total % count
let enabled: Bool = count > 0 && average >= 3.0
print(whole)
print(average)
print(remainder)
print(enabled)

Line six first compares count with zero, producing a Bool, then uses && to require the other comparison too. That operator short-circuits: the right expression is evaluated only if the left is true. Parentheses can clarify a compound expression. The printed values are 3, 3.5, 1 and true. Existing numeric variables of different types generally need explicit conversions before arithmetic. This resembles Kotlin’s explicit numeric conversions, but the platform width and available exactness rules differ. Double conversion may lose precision for large integers; a successful conversion does not prove an exact identifier round trip.

sections.title: Read each symbol as one question
sections.html:
An operator is a symbol that performs an operation. = assigns a value to a mutable binding. == asks whether two values are equal; != asks whether they differ. The four order comparisons ask less than, at most, greater than, or at least. Their result is Bool, meaning true or false. Swift requires a Bool condition: a count must be compared, not treated as truth by itself. Prefix ! reverses a Bool. condition ? yes : no evaluates only the selected answer.

A trap stops normal execution when a runtime rule is violated. Ordinary integer addition, subtraction, and multiplication trap on overflow, meaning the result cannot fit in the type. Common JVM integer operations instead wrap. Swift has explicit wrapping operators, but choosing them changes the number rule; it does not validate input. Division by zero also traps. Ordinary throws/catch does not recover these traps. Use safe known inputs here, and define bounds for external counts. Int8(exactly: value) returns nil for a value that cannot fit unchanged. Checking bounds and converting before arithmetic address separate risks.

sections.title: Count text using the unit you mean
sections.html:
A String is text. A Character is one extended grapheme cluster: the group of Unicode pieces Swift treats as one character. For example, an accented letter can use more than one Unicode piece. Swift String.count counts Characters; Java and Kotlin String length count UTF-16 code units, smaller encoding pieces. A complex emoji can therefore have different counts. If a limit is in UTF-8 bytes, use utf8.count. Bytes, code units, and visible characters answer different questions. Interpolation builds text using \(...); + joins strings.

Swift strings do not support an arbitrary integer subscript as though every character occupied one fixed-width slot. We will study collection indices separately; today use count and isEmpty. "" is a present empty String. Spaces are content too, so checking isEmpty does not reject whitespace-only input. Standard-library text operations require no Foundation import. More specialized localization or formatting may introduce Foundation and platform rules later. Kotlin string templates are a useful construction analogy, but their dollar syntax and representation assumptions should not be transplanted. A string constructed from a counter is a value, not reactive state; updating the counter will not rewrite it.

sections.title: Keep missing and empty separate
sections.html:
An optional can hold a value or no value. String? means either text or absence, spelled nil. An empty String is still present text. Nil coalescing, written ??, chooses a fallback only for absence. Thus absentCaption becomes Unknown, while blankCaption stays empty. An exact conversion checks whether a value fits without changing it. Int8(exactly: 200) returns nil because a signed eight-bit integer cannot hold 200. The example prints Unknown, true, and true.

let absent: String? = nil
let blank: String? = ""
let absentCaption = absent ?? "Unknown"
let blankCaption = blank ?? "Unknown"
let narrow: Int8? = Int8(exactly: 200)
print(absentCaption)
print(blankCaption.isEmpty)
print(narrow == nil)

Kotlin nullable types and the Elvis operator provide a conceptual bridge, but Swift optional handling uses its own syntax and explicit bindings in the next lesson. An optional is not the string "null", a zero, or an empty placeholder. Applying postfix ! forces an optional’s contained value and traps for nil; the examples deliberately preserve absence instead. Prefix ! negates a Bool, so placement changes meaning. Optional chaining and binding will let you consume a present value without changing the original domain fact. Do not erase a missing identifier merely to simplify display.

sections.title: Check the result as well as the type
sections.html:
A type error means the compiler rejects the expression. A wrong calculation may still compile. total + average mixes existing Int and Double values and needs an explicit conversion. Double(total / count) compiles but has already lost the fraction. Decide whether the requirement needs exact whole numbers or a fractional average before repairing it. Likewise, blank ?? "Unknown" keeps empty text. If the product requires empty text to show Unknown, write a separate content rule; absence is a different question.

In the active question model, key and prompt are String, subtitle is String?, and isOptional is Bool. These are separate scalar contracts in a real feature. Reading them does not tell you whether blank subtitles are accepted; a consumer must decide presentation behavior. In the active Array chunking helper, count > size guards a branch and a later conversion constructs Int from the requested size. Its signature uses UInt, an unsigned integer, so you must inspect input boundaries rather than assuming negative values or zero have a universal meaning. Our positive test inputs teach numeric intent; they are not a complete audit of that helper. Source membership is confirmed in ZDCore’s Project.swift.

exercise.brief: Calculate an average and compare missing, empty, and named labels. Keep exact conversion failures visible.
steps: Set total to Int seven and count to Int two. Predict the whole-number answer and the fractional answer.
Convert both operands to Double before division. Print both answers.
Make three String? inputs: nil, empty text, and Ada. Predict which uses the fallback.
Try exact Int8 conversion for 127 and 128. Keep the optional results.
Explain why a missing label and an empty label need separate validation rules.
acceptance: The fractional average is 3.5 rather than 3.0.
Nil selects Unknown; empty remains empty; Ada stays Ada.
127 converts exactly and 128 yields nil.
No force unwrap, overflow demonstration or division-by-zero execution is needed.
exercise.solution:
This answer runs as a standalone file. It keeps number conversion and label display decisions in view. No framework import or earlier declaration is required. Predict the seven outputs first. Check especially whether the empty String uses the fallback, and whether 128 fits in Int8.

let total = 7
let count = 2
print(total / count)
print(Double(total) / Double(count))
let absent: String? = nil
let blank: String? = ""
let named: String? = "Ada"
print(absent ?? "Unknown")
print((blank ?? "Unknown").isEmpty)
print(named ?? "Unknown")
print(Int8(exactly: 127) == 127)
print(Int8(exactly: 128) == nil)

The outputs are 3, 3.5, Unknown, true, Ada, true and true. Parentheses around blank’s fallback group the resulting nonoptional String before isEmpty is read. Exact conversion at the signed eight-bit upper boundary succeeds, and one step beyond it returns nil. None of this makes two hundred a valid booking count; the exercise checks representation, not a product rule.

For a real display rule that treats blank as invalid, state that policy separately and validate content before presenting a caption. Do not replace nil in a stored identifier with zero because the UI needs text. If the count could be zero, require a control-flow check before division; lesson 059 supplies that syntax. Record what your run established and which conditions you only predicted. The standalone scalar checks do not verify localization, network serialization, or any company model.

lessons.title: Choose branches and repeat work safely
lessons.summary: Choose what runs for each input, handle missing values, and make loops start and stop at the right points.
objectives: Read if, switch, while, repeat, and for-in as choices about what runs.
Use optional binding and explain where its new name can be read.
Predict range endpoints, empty loops, and steps between values.

sections.title: Turn a decision table into branches
sections.html:
Control flow is the order in which the program runs instructions. A branch chooses a path. In a form, one path handles a missing caption and another handles a present caption. A condition is an expression producing Bool, true or false. if checks it and runs the body between braces when true. else gives the other path. This resembles an Android decision table you already use. Swift usually needs no parentheses around a simple condition, but it still requires braces; indentation helps readers and does not replace them.

Start with one decision per branch. A nullable label needs an absence decision; a nonempty requirement needs a separate content decision. Counting slots needs boundaries, including zero. Combining these into a huge Boolean expression may compile, but it hides the rule you should test. Unlike some languages, Swift cannot treat zero or an empty string as false implicitly. Comparisons and isEmpty produce the needed Bool. These examples are synchronous standalone Swift: entering a branch does not schedule a job or update a UI. We are learning execution order before adding functions, collections, or framework callbacks.

sections.title: Use a present value inside its branch
sections.html:
Optional binding asks whether an optional holds a value and gives that value a usable name. if let name = input creates a nonoptional String named name only in the successful branch. It leaves input alone. Here input contains empty text, so name.isEmpty is true and the program prints Present but blank. A nonempty value takes the greeting path. Nil takes the outer else and prints Absent. Scope means where a name is available: name ends at its branch’s closing brace. The final print reads input and prints a blank line.

let input: String? = ""
if let name = input {
    if name.isEmpty {
        print("Present but blank")
    } else {
        print("Hello, \(name)")
    }
} else {
    print("Absent")
}
print(input ?? "Fallback")

Kotlin often smart-casts a stable nullable value after a null check. Swift optional binding makes a new binding explicit. The modern shorthand if let input unwraps an optional under the same name within the success branch; use the longer form while learning the scopes. A comma can combine optional binding with another condition, evaluated in order. Do not confuse a comma-separated condition with passing arguments to a function. A postfix force unwrap would avoid this branch syntax but would turn nil into a runtime trap. Write the intended absence behavior instead.

sections.title: Choose whether the endpoint is included
sections.html:
A range describes values between two bounds. A half-open range includes its start and excludes its end. 0..<3 gives zero, one, and two. A closed range includes both ends, so 1...3 gives one, two, and three. A for-in loop visits each value and gives it a local name for that iteration, one pass through the body. You do not increment that name yourself. Kotlin until and inclusive ranges express similar intent; use Swift’s own punctuation and types.

let slotCount = 3
for slot in 0..<slotCount {
    print("Index \(slot)")
}
for day in 1...3 {
    print("Day \(day)")
}
for minute in stride(from: 0, to: 15, by: 5) {
    print("Minute \(minute)")
}

Stride produces values with a step. From zero, stopping before fifteen, stepping by five gives zero, five and ten. The corresponding through overload includes an exactly reached end. Positive and negative steps express direction deliberately. A half-open 0..<0 is empty and performs no iterations; a closed range with lower bound greater than upper bound is invalid. Therefore 0...count - 1 is unsafe for a count of zero. Counts from untrusted input need a nonnegative validation rule too: half-open does not mean reversed bounds are generally legal. Prefer direct element iteration once you have an array, rather than building indices unnecessarily.

sections.title: Give every loop a way to progress
sections.html:
A while loop checks its condition before each pass, so it can run zero times. A repeat loop runs its body once before checking. This is like Kotlin while and do-while, with a different keyword. continue skips the rest of the current pass; break leaves the nearest loop. If the condition uses a counter, make sure every continuing path updates it. An update placed after continue never runs on that path, which can leave the condition true forever.

Guard checks a prerequisite and requires its else branch to leave the guarded scope. Inside a function, that can be return or throw. Inside a loop, break or continue can provide the required exit. guard candidate > 0 else { continue } skips this pass when candidate is not positive. A successful guard binding remains available afterward in that scope; an if-let binding is limited to its branch. Functions and return arrive in lesson 060, so today’s loops need no function declaration. Guard does not catch errors or provide automatic cleanup. Use it to make a required condition and its rejected path easy to see.

sections.title: Make a switch cover every value
sections.html:
A switch compares one value with patterns, rules describing which values match. Here zero matches the first case, ranges match the next cases, and default handles the rest. Seven prints Medium. An exhaustive switch covers every possible input; Swift requires this. The selected case finishes without entering the next one. You do not need Java’s usual break after each case. A break can express a branch that deliberately does nothing. Avoid fallthrough while learning: it enters the next body without testing its pattern again.

let score = 7
switch score {
case 0:
    print("None")
case 1...5:
    print("Small")
case 6...10:
    print("Medium")
default:
    print("Outside the taught range")
}
for candidate in -1...2 {
    guard candidate > 0 else { continue }
    print("Accepted \(candidate)")
}

The for loop demonstrates a guard that continues on minus one and zero, then prints Accepted 1 and Accepted 2. Guarding the prerequisite leaves the useful action unnested. For a later locally declared enum, explicit cases can cover every possible variant and make default unnecessary. That is where compiler coverage becomes especially useful. A broad default in a finite domain can hide a newly added decision. Today’s range matching does not cast classes or unpack tuples; those language constructs have their own lessons. Exhaustive matching checks possible inputs, not whether your messages are sensible or whether a workflow transition is allowed.

sections.title: Try zero, one, and several items
sections.html:
An off-by-one error includes or excludes one position by mistake. A range from zero through count includes count, which is one past an array’s last valid index. A while counter that never changes has a progress error. A guard is a prerequisite check whose failing branch must leave its scope; merely printing and falling through is a compiler error. These failures need different explanations. Predict behavior for zero, one, and several items before choosing punctuation. If a nested loop needs an outer exit, name that loop and explain why.

The active core array helper uses stride and half-open slices when chunking. We inspected its source and target inclusion, but its unsigned size argument still requires thought about zero and conversion; a real signature is evidence of code shape, not a universal correctness promise. The cancellation coordinator switches over its NavigationState at line 53, with associated payloads you will learn later. Read only the branch structure now. In the core sequence grouping helper, a guard continues when no grouping key exists. That policy deliberately omits elements without keys. Compare it with Kotlin continue: the role is similar, but Swift optional binding creates a concrete local key for the remaining body.

exercise.solution:
This answer runs as one file and needs no arrays or functions. The test inputs are values written directly into the program. Predict the output for slots zero and caption empty. Then try the same optional block with nil and Sam so each path gets its own check.

let slots = 0
for index in 0..<slots {
    print(index)
}
let caption: String? = ""
if let value = caption {
    print(value.isEmpty ? "Blank" : value)
} else {
    print("Absent")
}
var attempt = 0
while attempt < 2 {
    print("Attempt \(attempt)")
    attempt += 1
}

There are no index lines, followed by Blank, Attempt 0 and Attempt 1. The compound assignment += 1 is shorthand for reading the integer, adding one and assigning it back. It occurs before the next condition check and is not skipped by any branch. Changing slots to one yields one index line, zero. Changing caption to nil activates the outer else; changing it to Sam activates the nonempty selection.

A closed zero-through-minus-one range is invalid instead of being a clever way to skip the loop. An unchanged attempt would never make the condition false. Explain those outcomes on paper rather than running a hang or trap. For the repository guard, absence of a grouping key triggers continue and excludes that element, which is a business/utility policy in addition to a syntax choice. lessons.title: Give functions clear inputs and results
lessons.summary: Write reusable functions, read their argument labels, and return one value or a small group of values.
objectives: Tell a call-site label from the parameter name used inside the function.
Use return, guard, defaults, and distinct function signatures.
Return and unpack a tuple, and know when a named type would explain more.

sections.title: Name a rule you want to reuse
sections.html:
A function is a named operation you can call with inputs. A parameter is an input name inside its body; an argument is the value a caller supplies. A result is the value sent back. This is familiar from a Kotlin formatter or validator. In Swift, func begins the declaration, parentheses list inputs, an arrow names the result type, and braces hold the body. Declaring it does not run it. Calling today’s function runs its body synchronously, before the caller continues; the signature adds no suspension or other effects.

A function should expose the domain question being answered. A caption operation can return text without printing it. This separates calculation from an observable output and makes test inputs easier to compare. A guard can return an early fallback for missing input, leaving the remaining path with a validated nonoptional value. None of this requires an interface, dependency injection container, UIKit controller, or coroutine. Your Kotlin experience with pure helpers is useful, but Swift’s argument labels and immutable parameters have their own rules. Start with explicit names and return statements; terse expression bodies and overload tricks are less valuable than being able to explain a call.

sections.title: Read labels at the call and names in the body
sections.html:
An argument label is the name written at a call site. A parameter name is the name used inside the function. They can differ. In caption(for name:), the caller writes for and the body reads name. Attempt uses one name for both roles. Its default is one, used when the caller omits that argument. return supplies the result and exits the function. In twice, an underscore removes the external label; it does not remove the input. The body still reads the local value parameter.

func caption(for name: String, attempt: Int = 1) -> String {
    return "\(name): attempt \(attempt)"
}
func twice(_ value: Int) -> Int {
    return value * 2
}
let first = caption(for: "Sam")
let second = caption(for: "Sam", attempt: 2)
print(first)
print(second)
print(twice(3))

The first call omits attempt and uses the declared default. The second supplies attempt two. Neither call uses name:, because that is not the first external label. Twice is called as twice(3), not twice(value: 3). Output is Sam: attempt 1, Sam: attempt 2, and 6. Swift labels are part of the callable shape and often make APIs read like phrases. Kotlin named arguments generally use the declared parameter name; there is no direct equivalent to Swift independently spelling for and name. An underscore removes the label, not the argument itself.

sections.title: Return a result on every ordinary path
sections.html:
A return leaves the current function call and gives its result to the caller. Here the input type String? permits absence, but the result type String promises actual text on each ordinary exit. The first guard returns Hello for nil. The second returns Please add a name for present empty text. The last return greets a nonempty name. The guard binds a usable String after checking input. These are three domain rules, not one null check. Returning does not shut down the process or every surrounding caller.

func greeting(for input: String?) -> String {
    guard let name = input else {
        return "Hello"
    }
    guard !name.isEmpty else {
        return "Please add a name"
    }
    return "Hello, \(name)"
}
print(greeting(for: nil))
print(greeting(for: ""))
print(greeting(for: "Ada"))

Parameters are immutable bindings inside a function by default. Attempting input = nil or incrementing an Int parameter is rejected. Make a local var copy when you intend local mutation; inout for caller-visible mutation is taught in lesson 064. A function returning no useful value has result type Void, which Swift models as the empty tuple. Omitting the arrow/result type declares that form. Print itself is an output action, not a substitute for returning a calculated String. Swift checks ordinary return coverage, but a compiling function can still treat as the same absent and blank incorrectly if your branches encode the wrong policy.

sections.title: Return a small pair as a tuple
sections.html:
A tuple groups several values in parentheses. This result has two named Int parts, whole and remainder. The question mark after the tuple makes the entire pair optional. Guard returns nil for a nonpositive divisor before division occurs. On success, optional binding gives the caller the whole pair. Read its named members or unpack it into two local names; unpacking is called destructuring. An unnamed tuple can use .0, but named parts make a result easier to read. This is a language value, not Kotlin’s exact Pair class.

func division(_ total: Int, by count: Int) -> (whole: Int, remainder: Int)? {
    guard count > 0 else { return nil }
    return (whole: total / count, remainder: total % count)
}
if let result = division(7, by: 2) {
    print(result.whole)
    print(result.remainder)
    let (whole, remainder) = result
    print("\(whole), \(remainder)")
}
print(division(7, by: 0) == nil)

This resembles returning Kotlin Pair, yet a Swift tuple is a language compound value rather than the exact Kotlin Pair class/API. Tuple labels improve reading but do not replace a domain type with construction invariants, reusable methods, or explicit protocol conformances. For a small internal pair, a tuple is economical; once the result means a reusable concept, a struct may be preferable. The example assumes a modest positive divisor and total seven; integer minimum divided by minus one is deliberately avoided by its positive-divisor guard. Guarding zero alone would not prove every arithmetic combination safe. The output is 3, 1, then 3, 1 as one line, and true.

sections.title: Make omitted inputs and alternate calls easy to read
sections.html:
A default argument supplies a value when the caller omits that input. The parameter still exists. Use a default for a common choice, such as the first attempt; require an explicit input when the caller must make a meaningful decision, such as whether to overwrite data. Overloading gives several functions the same base name but different callable signatures. A signature is the shape of the inputs, labels, and result. Labels can help Swift choose the right call. If a caller cannot tell which overload is intended, simplify the API.

A variadic parameter accepts zero or more inputs of one type. In func count(_ values: Int...) -> Int { values.count }, values is an array inside the body. Arrays arrive in lesson 061; this is optional orientation rather than today’s prerequisite. Variadic inputs and defaults solve different problems. A function can also be stored as a value with a function type; closures and ownership arrive in lesson 068. Keep the calls direct for now. A default, tuple, or function name does not schedule background work. Throws permits failure; async permits suspension. A name such as load promises neither by itself.

sections.title: Check the declared label before calling
sections.html:
A call contract tells a caller how to invoke an operation and what to expect. The linked Set helper declares toggled(value:), using value both outside and inside. The Array helper declares resize(count target:), using count at the call and target inside. Its delete closure has a default; a closure is a function value you will study later. The grouping helper returns tuples with named key and values parts. Source patterns confirm these helpers belong to their targets. Reading their labels does not prove all possible inputs are safe.

A common invalid translation is caption(name: "Sam") because Kotlin encourages matching the parameter name. The correction is the declared external label for. A common behavioral error is printing inside a function intended to return a String and forgetting the return; the caller then lacks its promised result. Another is ignoring nil from an optional result and forcing the tuple, turning invalid input into a trap. Distinguish signature mistakes from domain mistakes. Write expected outputs at the call boundary before reading the helper’s body. That habit scales to unfamiliar client APIs without requiring the entire framework architecture.

exercise.solution:
This answer runs as a standalone file. It handles the tuple only after optional binding succeeds. The caption function returns text instead of printing it itself, so the caller controls output. Predict the five printed lines before running.

func distribute(_ total: Int, among count: Int) -> (whole: Int, remainder: Int)? {
    guard count > 0 else { return nil }
    return (total / count, total % count)
}
func caption(for name: String, suffix: String = "ready") -> String {
    return "\(name): \(suffix)"
}
if let parts = distribute(7, among: 2) {
    print(parts.whole)
    print(parts.remainder)
}
print(distribute(7, among: 0) == nil)
print(caption(for: "Rae"))
print(caption(for: "Rae", suffix: "waiting"))

Expected lines are 3, 1, true, Rae: ready and Rae: waiting. Tuple labels come from the declared return contract even though the return expression uses positional construction. The local name count is supplied under external among; total has no external label. Nil means this helper could not produce its result for the stated divisor, not that either component equals zero.

To test transfer, change the valid input to eight among three and predict two and two. Then state an additional domain rule, such as forbidding negative totals, and decide where to validate it. Do not assume positive divisor validation already covers that separate product requirement. Your own helper, predictions and observed run establish exercise evidence. These small synchronous operations do not establish service effects, actor isolation, or UI formatting correctness.

lessons.title: Keep arrays in order and edit copies safely
lessons.summary: Build ordered lists, handle empty lists, and explain which value changes after a copy or a slice.
objectives: Create and edit typed arrays while checking index bounds.
Choose element iteration or indices, and use a slice’s own index range.
Predict array value copies and explain why shared storage is not shared edits.

sections.title: Use an array when order matters
sections.html:
An Array is an ordered list whose entries all have one element type. [String] means a list of text values. Square brackets containing values create an array literal, a list written directly in source. A typed empty array such as let names: [String] = [] still has a known element type. This fits an Android result list that may contain repeated names. Array comes from Swift’s standard library and is a value type: assigning it gives observable value independence. You need no UI or Foundation import.

Kotlin List describes a read-only collection interface and MutableList permits mutation through that interface. Assigning a Kotlin mutable-list reference normally aliases its object. Swift Array assignment instead gives independent observable values. A let-bound Swift array cannot append or replace its elements; use var at a deliberate edit point. This difference is more substantial than replacing Kotlin val with Swift let. Neither model alone promises deep immutability of objects contained in the collection. We will define classes later; for now, String and Int elements make the independence directly observable. Repeated elements are valid unless your domain says otherwise, and an empty array is still a present collection.

sections.title: Follow each edit in order
sections.html:
Mutation means changing a value. Here the original array stays fixed under let, and edited can change under var. Append adds Rae at the end. Subscript assignment uses [1] to replace Lin with Sam. Insert adds Kai at zero and moves later positions forward. RemoveLast removes and returns Rae. The original remains Ada, Lin, Ada; edited becomes Kai, Ada, Sam, Ada. Duplicates remain because none of these operations removes them. An index is a position in this list, not a lasting identity for a person.

let original = ["Ada", "Lin", "Ada"]
var edited = original
edited.append("Rae")
edited[1] = "Sam"
edited.insert("Kai", at: 0)
let removed = edited.removeLast()
print(original)
print(edited)
print(removed)

Value semantics describes what callers can observe, not when every storage byte is copied. Arrays can share internal storage until an edit needs separation. This optimization is called copy-on-write, or COW. It preserves independent array values, but supplies no actor or lock for unsafe concurrent mutation. Subscript replacement requires an existing index. An insertion or removal can move positions, so a saved index may later name a different element or become invalid. A semantic identifier names the record itself; use that for lasting UI identity. A small output check establishes the edit result, not the allocation cost or thread safety.

sections.title: Treat an empty list as a normal input
sections.html:
An index identifies a position you can access. An empty array has no valid element indices, but isEmpty and count still work: they give true and zero. First returns an optional because the first element may not exist. Direct for-in iteration runs zero times for an empty array. For a populated array, indices gives precisely the current valid range, here zero and one. endIndex means the position after the last element. You cannot read an element there. If an input index can be negative, checking only that it is less than count is not enough.

let names: [String] = []
print(names.isEmpty)
print(names.count)
print(names.first ?? "No first name")
for name in names {
    print(name)
}
let populated = ["Ada", "Lin"]
for index in populated.indices {
    print("\(index): \(populated[index])")
}

Ordinary array[index] traps for an invalid position. It is not Kotlin getOrNull. removeFirst and removeLast require an element; popLast returns an optional when the array may be empty. An optional element and an absent first element are also separate questions. Recheck saved indices after structural edits. Direct element iteration is clearer when positions are unnecessary. Enumerated gives an offset and a value; that offset counts steps in the traversal and is not every collection’s actual Index. A slice may start at one or another retained source position. Use the collection’s own indices instead of assuming zero.

sections.title: Use the slice’s own positions
sections.html:
An ArraySlice is a part of an array that keeps the parent’s index coordinates. The slice names[1..<3] contains Lin and Rae at indices one and two. It does not start at zero. Reading tail[1] gives Lin; tail[0] is invalid. Array(tail) builds an Array whose indices start at zero, so standalone[0] gives Lin too. The start indices print one and zero. The element values match, but the two containers use different coordinates. A range must also fit the source before you can slice it.

let names = ["Ada", "Lin", "Rae", "Sam"]
let tail = names[1..<3]
print(tail.startIndex)
print(tail[1])
let standalone = Array(tail)
print(standalone.startIndex)
print(standalone[0])

A slice can share and retain the parent storage, so keeping a tiny slice of a large array may retain a larger allocation than expected. Converting to Array can be a useful ownership boundary for a long-lived small subset, but it is a choice with allocation costs, not automatic optimization advice. The range bounds must still be valid for the source. Slicing does not transform or validate elements, and constructing an Array of class references would not deep-clone their objects. Describe both index behavior and contained-value behavior when reviewing a helper. Today’s tiny test inputs verify observable results; they do not measure allocation sizes or client memory usage.

sections.title: Choose an edit from the rule it must follow
sections.html:
An edit contract says what should change and what should stay. Append adds one item; append(contentsOf:) adds several; replacing a range changes a span. Returning a new array lets the caller choose whether to keep it. An ordinary Array parameter is a value and cannot directly replace the caller’s variable. Lesson 064 adds inout for that purpose. reserveCapacity asks for room to grow; it does not add elements or change count. Front insertion moves later positions, so repeated front inserts can cost more as lists grow. Measure that cost if it matters.

Do not remove elements while assuming an old traversal’s positions remain correct. One safe beginner strategy is to construct a new array of kept elements using a for loop; filter later supplies a concise expression of that policy. Sorting returns or mutates an order, and removing duplicates needs a separate rule about which occurrence and order to preserve. Converting to Set will lose multiplicity and has no stable display order. Kotlin collection intuition is valuable for algorithm intent, but Swift’s value storage and slice coordinates remain independent facts. Distinguish a user-visible edit requirement from an incidental storage optimization when choosing the operation.

sections.title: Read what a helper actually preserves
sections.html:
A mutating method changes the value it is called on. The linked resize helper does that. Its resized partner makes a local copy, edits it, and returns the result, leaving the caller to choose what to store. Its duplicate-removal helper converts through Set, a collection of unique members. That removes repeats but promises no original display order. Check the implementation before telling a UI consumer its list order is preserved. The ZDCoreBase source pattern includes this file in the target; it is active source, not evidence of an executed test.

The question model has an options array, and the cancellation coordinator appends responses and removes the last one on an error path. These source observations connect ordered state with update policy, but proving all removal paths safe needs workflow context and tests. Our lesson does not supply that proof. Misconceptions to catch include reading an empty array by subscript without checking, treating endIndex as the last valid element, reading tail[0], and assuming assignment aliases a Kotlin MutableList. Predict the failure category: an invalid index is a runtime trap, while append on a let-bound Array is a compiler rejection. Neither is an ordinary thrown service error.

The two array prints differ only in the edited value. Both empty checks print true. Start indices print one and zero, and the final line is Lin. Contains is evaluated against the slice’s own indices, so it does not mistakenly authorize index zero. objectives: Look up, update, and remove dictionary entries, including default reads.

sections.title: Pick a list, a lookup table, or a membership group
sections.html:
A Dictionary connects a key with a value. [String: Int] maps text keys to whole-number counts. A Set keeps unique members; Set<String> keeps unique text values. The angle brackets supply the element type, called a type argument. An Array keeps ordered entries, including repeats. These answer different questions in an Android model: list the results, find the count for a specialty, or ask whether an ID is selected. You can use these standard containers before learning how to write generics. They need no Foundation import.

Dictionary keys and Set elements must support Hashable, a standard-library contract that includes value equality and hashing. A hash helps locate possible matches; equality still determines whether keys/elements are the same. Hash collisions between unequal values are permitted and do not make them equal. A hash value is not a durable record identifier and must not be persisted as though stable across runs. Kotlin Map/Set are useful shape analogies, but Swift’s standard Dictionary and Set have value semantics. Their traversal order is not a declared display order. Use an Array or explicitly sort output when a product requires a deterministic presentation.

sections.title: Update one key and notice what is absent
sections.html:
A dictionary association is one key linked to one value. The literal starts with general linked to two. Assigning counts to original preserves that value. The default subscript supplies zero when needed, and += 1 writes the updated count back. Assigning dental creates its entry; looking up vision gives nil because it is missing. Ordinary lookup returns Int? for this reason. Assigning nil removes dental. The output is 3, true, true, and 2. The printed minus-one fallback is not saved as an entry.

var counts: [String: Int] = ["general": 2]
let original = counts
counts["general", default: 0] += 1
counts["dental"] = 4
let missing = counts["vision"]
print(counts["general"] ?? -1)
print(missing == nil)
counts["dental"] = nil
print(counts["dental"] == nil)
print(original["general"] ?? -1)

Each equal key has one stored value. Reassignment replaces its value rather than adding another entry with that key. A default read such as counts["unknown", default: 0] can supply zero without storing an entry. In our Int example, += 1 mutates the value through the subscript, so the updated count is written back. Reference-valued dictionaries require care: changing a property of a returned object need not assign that object into a missing entry. Do not infer insertion from a reached object’s mutation. Unlike an array’s out-of-bounds access, an ordinary dictionary lookup for a missing key simply returns nil.

sections.title: Separate no key from a key with no payload
sections.html:
A payload is the value stored for an existing key. In [String: Int], lookup returns Int? to express whether the key exists. In [String: Int?], the payload can also be absent, so lookup returns Int??. The outer optional answers whether there is an entry; the inner optional answers whether that entry has an integer. These are separate questions. Nested optionals can be useful, but a named state such as unknown or known often explains the domain better. First make sure you can tell which question each layer answers.

In an optional-valued dictionary, values["a"] = nil removes the key: it sets the outer optional to absence. To keep the entry but store no integer, use updateValue(nil, forKey: "a") or explicitly supply a present outer optional with a nil payload. Optional binding of a lookup can confirm the entry exists while its inner payload remains nil. Kotlin Map.get can also mix up missing entries and nullable values unless you check containsKey. Swift shows the two optional layers in the type. Test deletion and an unknown stored payload separately before applying a fallback.

sections.title: State how duplicates combine and how output is ordered
sections.html:
A duplicate-key policy says what to do when inputs name the same key more than once. This histogram counts every occurrence. A histogram is a lookup table of counts. The empty dictionary literal is [:]. Each general input increments its count, so general becomes two and dental one. Sorting the keys makes the printed order dental then general. A dictionary’s incidental traversal order is not your presentation rule. Sorting the output does not alter which value belongs to each key.

let labels = ["general", "dental", "general"]
var histogram: [String: Int] = [:]
for label in labels {
    histogram[label, default: 0] += 1
}
for key in histogram.keys.sorted() {
    if let count = histogram[key] {
        print("\(key): \(count)")
    }
}

Some initializers require unique input keys and trap if duplicates are supplied. Others accept a combining closure so you can define how conflicts resolve. Closures are taught in lessons 063 and 068; today’s explicit loop makes the combining rule visible without that prerequisite. Common choices include first wins, last wins, aggregate, or reject. Pick one from the business rule and test duplicate inputs. Silent overwrite can conceal data loss when a producer adds a second record with the same key. A map keyed by display name is especially fragile if equal names represent different records. Hashing does not fix a mistaken identity choice.

sections.title: Ask membership questions with a set
sections.html:
Membership asks whether a value belongs to a group. A Set keeps one copy of each equal value, so repeated Ada produces one member. Insert returns information including inserted, which says whether a new member was added. Remove returns an optional removed member, and contains returns Bool. Intersection keeps members present in both groups; union includes members from either. Here the original count is two, Rae is newly inserted, and selected contains Rae. Sorting the intersection and union only makes their printed presentation stable.

var selected: Set<String> = ["Ada", "Lin", "Ada"]
let original = selected
let insertion = selected.insert("Rae")
selected.remove("Lin")
let visible: Set<String> = ["Ada", "Sam"]
print(original.count)
print(insertion.inserted)
print(selected.contains("Rae"))
print(selected.intersection(visible).sorted())
print(selected.union(visible).sorted())

This resembles Kotlin set operations, but assigning selected to original preserves an independent Set value rather than necessarily aliasing a mutable-set instance. A Set has no first-insertion display-order guarantee. Turning an ordered Array into Set loses duplicates and may lose the original order; turning it back does not reconstruct them. If the domain needs first-occurrence order, maintain an output Array and a seen Set together, as the active unique helper does. Mutating equality/hash-defining state of a referenced key while it is stored can undermine lookup invariants; define keys from stable value data. Custom Hashable implementations are further practice, not required today.

sections.title: Check the helper’s duplicate rule
sections.html:
A helper’s name is a clue; its body gives the rule. Set.toggled copies its value, removes a present member or adds a missing member, and returns the result. Sequence.unique uses a seen Set to detect repeated keys and an Array to retain the first chosen entries in input order. That preserves more than Set conversion alone. Dictionary helpers name overwrite and combining policies in their parameters. Those policies decide which data survives. Source patterns include these helpers in the active targets; our lesson does not claim to have run all their algorithms.

Misconceptions include treating a missing key as a stored zero, treating a default read as proof of insertion, expecting Set to preserve UI ordering, and using hashValue as a persistent ID. Identify the likely symptom for each: a hidden absent-data state, a surprising count/membership result, presentation that can vary between runs, or incompatible saved identifiers across runs. The source globs for ZDCoreBase and ZDCorePlusSentry confirm the inspected helpers belong to active targets. We do not import those targets into this lesson or claim their full algorithms were tested. Your standalone test inputs should show the collision rule and display order you chose.

exercise.brief: Count repeated labels and keep one copy of each label in first-appearance order.
steps: Use the text labels general, dental, general, vision in that order.
Count each label with a Dictionary default subscript.
Use a seen Set and an output Array. Append a label only the first time it appears.
Print counts by sorted key. Keep the unique list in input order.
Show the difference between an absent key and an existing key whose count is zero.
acceptance: General count is two; dental and vision counts are one.
Unique output is general, dental, vision in first-occurrence order.
An absent key remains nil rather than silently becoming stored zero.
The explanation states collision and presentation-order policies.
exercise.solution:
This answer runs on its own and uses the syntax introduced so far. Set.insert returns a tuple; its inserted member tells you whether this label is new. That lets you append first occurrences without a second lookup. Predict the sorted count lines and the ordered unique list separately.

let labels = ["general", "dental", "general", "vision"]
var counts: [String: Int] = [:]
var seen: Set<String> = []
var ordered: [String] = []
for label in labels {
    counts[label, default: 0] += 1
    if seen.insert(label).inserted {
        ordered.append(label)
    }
}
for key in counts.keys.sorted() {
    if let value = counts[key] { print("\(key): \(value)") }
}
print(ordered)
counts["empty"] = 0
print(counts["absent"] == nil)
print(counts["empty"] == 0)

The histogram prints dental one, general two and vision one in sorted-key order. Ordered contains general, dental and vision in their first appearance order, independent of set traversal. Both final checks print true, while the dictionary states they test differ: absent has no association; empty has a present zero.

To test transfer, begin the input with vision and confirm that the unique output begins with vision while the sorted histogram still begins with dental. That checks the two ordering contracts independently. If duplicate labels should be rejected rather than counted, state a different rule before changing implementation. The present exercise validates made-up value behavior and does not establish production identifier correctness or benchmark hashing performance.

lessons.title: Transform collections and know when work runs
lessons.summary: Read collection transformations as small rules. Track retained values, dropped values, result shapes, and deferred work.
objectives: Read a closure before passing it to map, filter, compactMap, or flatMap.
Choose how many results to keep and how to report invalid input.
Follow a reduction and explain why a lazy recipe does not cache its results.

sections.title: Explain the loop before shortening it
sections.html:
A pipeline passes values through a series of operations. You may already chain map and filter in Kotlin. Start by describing the equivalent loop: which inputs are visited, what gets kept, and what happens to invalid data? A shorter expression must keep the same rule. The result shape means whether you get one value per input, fewer values, nested values, or one final total. Timing matters too: eager work runs now; lazy work waits for a consumer. These standard-library operations are synchronous. The name map does not mean work runs concurrently.

A closure is an unnamed function value that can be passed to another operation. Its inputs and result follow a function type, such as (Int) -> Int. Braces surround its definition, in separates parameter declarations from the body, and the body may return a value. We introduce just the closure syntax needed to transform local values here. Storage, escaping and ownership are taught separately in lesson 068. The standard eager Array operations produce new arrays. Kotlin collection operations provide a useful algorithm analogy, but do not assume Swift’s generic Sequence means a lazy Kotlin Sequence.

sections.title: Give map a value rule and filter a yes-or-no rule
sections.html:
A closure is an unnamed function value. (Int) -> Int says one integer enters and one integer returns. In braces, value names the local input and in starts the body. Passing double to map tells it what to do for each element. Map preserves input order and produces one output per input, so the result is [2, 4, 6, 8]. Filter’s closure answers Bool: keep this original value or leave it out. The trailing closure is written after filter rather than inside the call’s parentheses.

let values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let double: (Int) -> Int = { value in
    return value * 2
}
let doubled = values.map(double)
let even = values.filter { value in
    return value % 2 == 0
}
print(doubled)
print(even)

Filter’s closure returns Bool and decides whether the original element is retained. It does not replace that element with true or false. Even is [2, 4]. With a single expression, a closure can omit return; Swift can infer its parameter/result types from the surrounding operation. Shorthand $0 means the first implicit closure parameter and $1 the second. Use explicit names until you can read the full rule. Kotlin often uses it for a single lambda parameter; Swift does not. A trailing closure is ordinary function-value syntax, not a special concurrent block. Map preserves multiplicity unless your transform itself changes the values.

sections.title: Keep absence or remove it deliberately
sections.html:
A failable initializer can return no value for unsuitable input. Int(text) returns Int? because bad is not an integer string. Map keeps every position, so attempts contains three optional entries, one nil. CompactMap removes nil results and returns [3, 8]. That is a data policy, not just a shorter spelling. A form may need to keep the failed text and explain it. FlatMap here joins each returned group into one array, giving [1, 2, 3]. It removes one nesting layer; it does not report errors or recursively flatten everything.

let texts = ["3", "bad", "8"]
let attempts: [Int?] = texts.map { text in Int(text) }
let valid: [Int] = texts.compactMap { text in Int(text) }
let groups = [[1, 2], [], [3]]
let flattened = groups.flatMap { group in group }
print(attempts.count)
print(valid)
print(flattened)

FlatMap in this example accepts a transform producing a sequence for each input group, then concatenates the elements into one array. The result is [1, 2, 3]. It flattens one nesting layer; it does not recursively flatten arbitrary data or automatically skip domain errors. Historical Swift code sometimes used flatMap for optional removal; modern explicit compactMap makes today’s intention clearer. Kotlin mapNotNull resembles compactMap’s shape, and flatMap has a related flattening role, but neither analogy chooses your error policy. Map with an optional-returning transform is not a compile error: [Int?] may be exactly what the consumer needs.

sections.title: Carry one answer through the inputs
sections.html:
An accumulator is the answer built up as each input arrives. Reduce begins with an initial value and calls its closure with the current accumulator and the next element. For zero and [1, 2, 3], the successive totals are one, three, and six. Empty input returns the starting value, so an empty reduction starting at ten returns ten. The order can matter: subtraction and concatenation are not freely reorderable. Input limits still matter too; reduce does not make integer addition immune to overflow.

let values = [1, 2, 3]
let sum = values.reduce(0) { total, value in
    return total + value
}
let labels = ["a", "b", "a"]
let counts = labels.reduce(into: [String: Int]()) { counts, label in
    counts[label, default: 0] += 1
}
print(sum)
print(counts["a"] ?? -1)
print([Int]().reduce(10) { total, value in total + value })

Reduce(into:) gives its closure temporary mutable access to the accumulator. Change it in place rather than returning a replacement. The typed empty dictionary sets up text keys and integer counts; the default subscript increments each label’s count. This can avoid repeatedly making replacement collection values. It remains synchronous and provides no synchronization for shared concurrent access. Kotlin fold helps explain the running-answer idea, but into has its own mutation rule, connected to inout in lesson 064. Choose the clearer form for the required output. A for loop is useful when errors or intermediate evidence need explicit handling; claim speed only after measuring relevant code.

sections.title: Separate a lazy recipe from saved results
sections.html:
Lazy means defer producing elements until a consumer asks for them. A lazy adapter wraps the source and describes how to get those elements. Creating this mapped pipeline does not call the transform, so visits starts at zero. Making an Array from its first two values gives [10, 20] and two visits in this example. Asking for those values again repeats the mapping and raises visits to four. Memoization means saving computed answers for later reuse; this adapter does not do that. Save the materialized Array if you need a result snapshot.

let values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
var visits = 0
let pipeline = values.lazy.map { value in
    visits += 1
    return value * 10
}
print(visits)
let firstTwo = Array(pipeline.prefix(2))
print(firstTwo)
print(visits)
let firstTwoAgain = Array(pipeline.prefix(2))
print(firstTwoAgain)
print(visits)

The visit counter makes evaluation visible. Prefer transforms without side effects: repeated lazy traversal may call them again, and different adapters may visit inputs differently. Do not assume every lazy filter has this exact visit count. Sequence is Swift’s iteration protocol, the capability to supply values in a traversal. Some sequences are single-pass and cannot be replayed safely; arrays can be traversed again. Sorting needs the relevant values and produces an eager result. A lazy prefix cannot make an arbitrary global sort inspect only two inputs. Kotlin Sequence helps explain deferred work, but Swift Sequence is broader; lazy is an explicit adapter.

sections.title: Read each intermediate result type
sections.html:
An intermediate type describes the values between two steps of a chain. The linked flatSorted helper first removes elements with missing sort keys using compactMap. It then sorts key/element tuples and maps back to elements. That is where missing-key rows disappear. A key path names a property to read; its syntax is separate further study. The selectedOption helper filters selected entries, then asks for the sole item, meaning exactly one. That policy differs from taking the first selected item and ignoring the others.

Misconceptions include expecting filter to produce Bools, assuming compactMap reports parse failures, expecting a lazy adapter to cache, and treating all Sequence operations as lazy. Rewrite a suspect chain as a loop and label each intermediate type. A valid pipeline can still lose required data: converting bad input to nil and dropping it may hide a validation error. If ordering matters, check where a sort or set conversion enters the chain. We verified these repository helpers and their source membership, but did not benchmark them or establish asynchronous behavior. The standalone exercise measures only its specified local outputs and evaluation counts.

exercise.brief: Parse quantity strings, count rejected input, and compare immediate work with repeated lazy consumption.
steps: Use the strings "2", "bad", and "5". Make both mapped optionals and compacted integers.
Explain which input was rejected and why counting only valid results hides it.
Sum valid integers with reduce. Also try empty input with initial zero.
Build a lazy doubled prefix and count transform calls.
Consume it twice. Explain repeated work without treating the call count as a general performance measurement.
acceptance: The mapped result has three positions and the compacted result is [2, 5].
The valid sum is seven and an empty sum with initial zero is zero.
A lazy adapter performs no mapping until consumed.
The answer explicitly reports one invalid input instead of treating dropped data as full success.
exercise.solution:
This answer runs as one file and prints each result shape. It counts rejected inputs for these test inputs; it is not a full error model that names every rejected row. Predict the outputs before running. Notice that the counter stays zero until the lazy result is consumed.

let texts = ["2", "bad", "5"]
let attempts = texts.map { text in Int(text) }
let valid = texts.compactMap { text in Int(text) }
print(attempts.count)
print(valid)
print(attempts.count - valid.count)
print(valid.reduce(0) { total, value in total + value })
print([Int]().reduce(0) { total, value in total + value })
var calls = 0
let doubled = valid.lazy.map { value in
    calls += 1
    return value * 2
}
print(calls)
print(Array(doubled.prefix(1)))
print(Array(doubled.prefix(1)))
print(calls)

The output is three, [2, 5], one, seven, zero, zero, [4], [4], two. Both materializations request the first mapped value again. Map retained the rejected position, while compactMap removed it. A user-facing parser should usually preserve which original text failed and the reason, rather than only a count; lesson 067 introduces enum/error representations for that purpose.

For retrieval, change bad to a valid three and predict the new count and sum before running. Then explain whether your product should reject an entire batch or accept valid entries with explicit rejection evidence. The language operations permit either policy; they do not choose it. A passing made-up pipeline does not verify real networking, asynchronous cancellation, performance or learner mastery.
